text.content:
This is unmistakably the heart of the warren: a wide, deliberately overcrowded chamber, every surface draped in fleece and hung with looted finery. At the far end, on a throne built entirely from stacked, buckled saddlebags, sits a llama - calm, well-groomed, and wearing a crude circlet of raw wool with genuine dignity. Standing beside the throne, close enough to touch it and clearly the one actually running things, is a figure that used to be a goblin: ashen-skinned now, small dark horns budding at the temples, eyes gone a starless black that doesn't quite track like an eye should. A crack in the floor behind the throne exhales cold, stale air from somewhere much deeper than this warren has any business reaching.

GM Notes

Objective: The stairwell down to the next floor is through that crack - the ward on it (see Hazard below) is the last thing standing between the party and it, and Corvin is standing between the party and the ward.

Milestone - the reveal: The Wool-Crowned King the whole floor has been talking about is, genuinely and sincerely, a llama named Buttercup - the goblins' worship of her is not a joke to them and doesn't need to be dismantled by the party at all. The real threat is Corvin Blackwell, once an unremarkable drover, who dared a friend into a fall off a llama's back and landed on something buried in the yard behind him: a golden hook shaped wrong for anything it could plausibly be used for. He picked it up. He has not put it down since. It changed him - Void Gaze, Reality Warp, a mind that increasingly narrates itself in the third person as "the Wool-Crowned King" - and it is, slowly and without any goblin noticing, changing the warren around him too: the nuzzle-hierarchy, the petting-zoo throne room, the sheer intensity of the llama worship, all of it downstream of whatever the hook is actually for.

Say, once combat starts or the party gets close: Corvin refers to himself exclusively in the third person as "the King," and to Buttercup with total, unfeigned reverence - he is not play-acting the throne-room theater, he believes every part of it, right up until the artifact's influence and his own dawning terror at what's happening to his hands start to show through the cracks.

Non-combat option: If the party recovered Old Tam's journal (Room 0) and pieced together its warning (a scattered clue trail also touches Rooms 6 and 24), they'll know Tam kept the hook quiet for decades with nothing more than an old counting-rhyme sung at it - a ritual so mundane Corvin's goblin instincts never flagged it as a threat. Singing it at Corvin mid-fight (or before it starts, if they're bold) should stagger his Void-granted abilities for a few rounds at your discretion - long enough to talk him down, drag him off the artifact, or just get a clean opening. This is a reward for investigation, not a requirement - the fight is winnable without it.

Hazard: A ward etched into the doorway/crack reacts to anyone not already marked as an ally (DC 14 to detect and counter) - unlike the warren's other wards, this one isn't goblin work at all. It's part of whatever the artifact is doing, and it gets more insistent, not less, the closer Corvin is to death.

Aftermath: Killing or subduing Corvin doesn't touch Buttercup's throne, and the goblins won't necessarily thank the party for it - as far as most of them are concerned, the King simply "changed his shape again," which by warren logic he's clearly allowed to do. What the party does with the hook itself is a hook (pun intended) for whatever's on the next floor down.
